lead: An electricity bill is not just units used. The tariff turns meter units into rupees using fixed and energy charges, often with slabs. An energy audit lists loads, measures kWh and finds where money leaks. A rooftop solar plant is sized from monthly kWh, panel wattage and peak sun hours, and net metering lets the grid absorb surplus. One unit on the meter is 1 kWh: the energy of a 1 kW load running for 1 hour.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.2 for energy meter reading, Chapter 6.4 for solar as a source, and Chapter 6.5 for distribution and the meter.

sections.h3: Tariff: from meter units to rupees

blocks.text: A tariff is the rule book that converts meter units into a bill. It exists because the electricity board must recover fixed costs such as wires and meters, plus running costs such as fuel, even when a home uses little power. A factory and a home pay different tariffs because their load shapes differ.
Bill = fixed charge + Σ(slab rate × slab kWh) + fuel surcharge + PF penalty − rebate
blocks.where: Σ means sum over slabs; slab rate is ₹ per kWh in that slab; slab kWh is the units in that slab; PF penalty is the power-factor charge; rebate is any credit.

items: Fixed charge is ₹ per month for the connection. A home with zero units still pays it.
Energy charge is ₹ per kWh, often in slabs: the first 100 kWh at one rate, the next 100 kWh at a higher rate.
Fuel surcharge is a ₹ per kWh adjustment when fuel prices change.
Power factor penalty applies to large consumers. Low power factor means more current for the same kW, so the tariff penalises PF below a limit, often 0.90.

blocks.text: A 100 W fan running for 10 hours uses 1 kWh. If the energy charge is ₹7 per kWh, that fan costs ₹7 for those 10 hours, before fixed charges. Tariff orders are public documents; read the one for your state rather than guessing slab rates.

sections.h3: Energy audit: find the high-use loads

blocks.text: An energy audit is a systematic check of where electricity is used and what can be cut without hurting comfort or work. It exists because most homes do not know which appliance drives the bill. The audit turns guesses into ranked kWh numbers.

items: List every load: lamp, fan, refrigerator, geyser, air conditioner, pump. Note its wattage from the nameplate and its hours per day.
Compute monthly kWh for each load from the formula below.
Read the energy meter at the start and end of a normal week. Compare the meter kWh with your list to catch missing loads.
Rank loads by monthly kWh. Usually the air conditioner, geyser and refrigerator come first, not lamps.
Estimate saving for each fix: LED lamps, five-star fans, AC setpoint at 26 °C, removing standby power, or a solar water heater.

blocks.where: W is load power in watts; h is hours per day; d is days per month; 1000 converts Wh to kWh.

blocks.text: A 1500 W geyser used 1 hour daily for 30 days uses (1500 × 1 × 30) ÷ 1000 = 45 kWh per month. At ₹7 per kWh it costs ₹315. A 60 W fan used 8 hours daily uses 14.4 kWh, about ₹101. The geyser is the better audit target.

sections.h3: Rooftop solar: size, inverter and net metering

blocks.text: A rooftop solar plant has panels that make DC, an inverter that changes DC to AC, and a net meter that records both import from the grid and export to it. Size the array from daily kWh need and local sun, not from roof area alone.
Daily kWh = array kW × PSH × PR
blocks.where: array kW is panel capacity in kW; PSH is peak sun hours, numerically hours at 1 kW/m²; PR is performance ratio, a fraction such as 0.80 for heat and wiring losses.

blocks.text: Panel count = array kW ÷ panel kW
blocks.where: panel kW is one panel's rating in kW, for example 500 W = 0.5 kW.

blocks.text: The inverter's AC rating is chosen close to the array kW, after checking its datasheet and DC/AC ratio. A grid-tied inverter is needed for net metering. A subsidy is often ₹ per kW but may be capped by kW or by a total amount. Net cost = cost − subsidy.
Net import kWh = import kWh − export kWh
blocks.where: import is grid energy used; export is surplus solar sent to the grid. The energy charge is normally on net import, not on total solar generation. Some syllabi call net metering net billing loosely; strictly, net billing pays export at a separate rate.

blocks.text: Payback in months = net cost ÷ monthly saving
blocks.where: net cost is ₹ after subsidy; monthly saving is ₹ per month from avoided grid units.

figure.caption: Solar panels make DC, the inverter makes AC, and the net meter sends solar to home loads first; surplus exports to the grid, while a deficit imports from it.

spec.title: Rooftop solar and net metering
spec.aria: Solar panels feed an inverter and a net meter; the meter supplies home loads and can export surplus to the grid or import a deficit.

examples.question: A home uses 300 kWh per month. It plans a 3 kW rooftop system using 500 W panels. Average generation is 4 kWh per kW per day for 30 days. Find the panel count, monthly generation and simple payback. Cost is ₹60,000 per kW, subsidy is ₹15,000 per kW, saved energy is valued at ₹7 per kWh for 300 kWh per month, and export credit is ignored.
steps: Array size = 3 kW. One panel = 500 W = 0.5 kW. Panel count = 3 ÷ 0.5 = 6 panels.
Daily generation = 3 kW × 4 kWh per kW per day = 12 kWh per day. Monthly generation = 12 × 30 = 360 kWh.
Billed saving uses 300 kWh per month; the extra 60 kWh is export and is ignored. Monthly saving = 300 × ₹7 = ₹2,100.
examples.answer: The plant needs 6 panels of 500 W, generates 360 kWh per month, costs ₹1,35,000 after subsidy, saves ₹2,100 per month, and has a simple payback of 64.3 months.
examples.check:
array_kw = 3
panel_w = 500
panel_kw = panel_w / 1000
panels = array_kw / panel_kw
daily_per_kw = 4
days = 30
monthly_gen = array_kw * daily_per_kw * days
cost = 60000 * array_kw
subsidy = 15000 * array_kw
net_cost = cost - subsidy
monthly_kwh_used = 300
rate = 7
saving = monthly_kwh_used * rate
payback = net_cost / saving
print(int(panels))
print(monthly_gen)
print(net_cost)
print(saving)
print(round(payback, 1))

traps: kW is power and kWh is energy. A 3 kW array does not make 3 kWh per hour unless the sun is at 1 kW/m² and losses are ignored.
A subsidy of ₹15,000 per kW may be capped after a certain kW or by a total amount. Read the scheme, not just the per-kW rate.
Net metering needs a grid-tied inverter and a bidirectional net meter. An off-grid solar system gets no export credit.
The energy charge is on net import, not on total solar generation. Export may be credited at a lower rate or carried forward.
Fixed charges and fuel surcharge can remain even when solar cuts units to zero. Power factor penalty is not for a typical home.

quiz.q: Define one unit of electricity in kWh.
quiz.a: One unit is 1 kWh, the energy used by a 1 kW load for 1 hour.

quiz.q: Name two parts of a tariff bill besides the energy charge.
quiz.a: Fixed charge and fuel surcharge; power factor penalty is another.

quiz.q: Why does an energy audit rank loads by monthly kWh rather than by wattage alone?
quiz.a: A high-wattage load used briefly can use less than a low-wattage load used for many hours. Monthly kWh combines power and time, so it matches the bill.

quiz.q: A 2 kW array gets 4.5 kWh per kW per day. Find daily kWh.
A 5 kW system costs ₹55,000 per kW and gets ₹18,000 per kW subsidy. Find net cost.
In a net-metered month a home imports 250 kWh and exports 60 kWh. On what kWh is the energy charge normally computed?
quiz.a: On net import = 250 − 60 = 190 kWh. Export is a credit, not total generation, and exact carry-forward rules vary.

quiz.q: Why can a 3 kW array with a 3 kW inverter export at midday while home loads are small?
quiz.a: Solar first supplies home loads. Any surplus flows through the grid-tied inverter and net meter to the grid, if export is approved.

beyond: Not for the exam. Time-of-day tariffs charge more at peak hours and less at night, so solar savings can exceed a flat ₹7 per kWh. Smart meters record import and export in intervals, enabling remote audits and automatic billing. Net billing and battery storage are changing payback calculations. Search for state tariff orders, net-metering regulations, and rooftop solar subsidy schemes.
